deep handler can only throw out of its own install site, above any tool loop, never back into the tool that
performed `session`, so the tool must be able to read the failure.

declarations.documentation:
Open a fresh e2b sandbox and return the sidecar's result: `{ ok: true, session }` — the id every later
call replays to reach the same sandbox — or `{ ok: false, message }` when the sandbox could not be opened.
declarations.name: e2b_open
declarations.signature: external agent e2b_open(api_key: string of private) -> unknown

declarations.documentation:
Run Python in the sandbox named by @session@ and return the sidecar's result: `{ ok: true, output }` with
its stdout / value / error text, or `{ ok: false, message }` on a sidecar-level failure. The sidecar
reconnects to that sandbox — recreating it under the same handle if it has expired — so state from earlier
calls in the same session survives everything but an actual expiry.
declarations.name: e2b_run_in
declarations.signature: external agent e2b_run_in(session: string, code: string, api_key: string of private) -> unknown

declarations.documentation:
Write @content@'s bytes into the sandbox named by @session@ at @path@ and return the sidecar's result:
`{ ok: true, path }` with the path e2b reports it wrote (missing directories are created, an existing file
is overwritten), or `{ ok: false, message }` when the write did not happen. The bytes travel over the
runtime's blob side channel: a `file` argument crosses the FFI boundary as a slim handle the sidecar
downloads.
declarations.name: e2b_put_file
declarations.signature: external agent e2b_put_file(session: string, path: string, content: file, api_key: string of private) -> unknown

declarations.documentation:
Read the bytes at @path@ out of the sandbox named by @session@ and return the sidecar's result:
`{ ok: true, content }` where `content` is a fresh `file` the sidecar uploaded back over the blob side
channel (owned by this call, so it ascends to the caller on return), or `{ ok: false, message }` when there
was nothing to read. @content_type@ is the MIME type to record on the new file ("" to record none): a
sandbox filesystem stores nothing about a file's type, so it has to be stated.
declarations.name: e2b_get_file
declarations.signature: external agent e2b_get_file(session: string, path: string, content_type: string, api_key: string of private) -> unknown

declarations.documentation:
The ambient e2b environment capability: the sandbox id and api key a tool runs against, as an outcome —
`session_ready(environment)` or `session_unavailable(message)`. The provider opens the sandbox lazily on
the first request and shares it after; an open failure comes back as `session_unavailable`, a value the
tool reads, rather than a throw from the provider's install site. Every tool performs it and matches on
the outcome before touching the sandbox.
declarations.name: session

declarations.checkedType: agent(continuation: agent(value: null) -> T0 with session | E1, source: env | oauth) -> T0 with throw[missing_secret | server_error] | E1 | io
declarations.documentation:
Provide an e2b environment for the extent of the continuation: one sandbox, opened lazily on the first
`session` request and shared by every tool call after, so the model's steps build on each other's state.
The session lives as long as this provider scope, so wrapping a single turn in its own
`use e2b.provider(...)` gives per-turn isolation. @source@ is a credential name, resolved at each `session`
request, so a rotation lands on the next tool call without a restart.
declarations.name: provider
declarations.signature: agent provider[R, effect E](source: credentials.source, continuation: agent(value: null) -> R with {...E, session}) -> R with E | io | prelude.throw[env.missing_secret | oauth.server_error]

declarations.checkedType: agent(code: string) -> string with session | throw[run_failed | sandbox_unavailable] | io
declarations.documentation:
Tool: execute Python code and return its output, in a persistent sandbox shared across this
conversation — variables, imports, and files you defined in earlier calls are still available, so build on
them instead of repeating work (if something you expected is missing, just define it again). A Python
error in your code is ordinary output: the traceback comes back as the result, to read and fix. What
throws is the sandbox itself failing — `sandbox_unavailable` when it could not be opened, `run_failed`
when it would not run the code — which a tool loop hands back to you as a message to work around.
declarations.name: run_python

declarations.checkedType: agent(content: file, path: string) -> string with session | throw[put_failed | sandbox_unavailable] | io
declarations.documentation:
Tool: put a file from this conversation into the Python sandbox, so code can open it — the only way an
attachment reaches Python. Pass the file's handle object as @content@ — a bare {"$katari_ref": "<id>"}
suffices (copy the id from the conversation) — and the @path@ to write it to (an absolute path such as
"/home/user/data.csv"; a relative one resolves against the sandbox's working directory), where missing
directories are created and an existing file is overwritten. Comes back as the path e2b actually wrote to,
so open that one from `run_python`, not the one you asked for; it throws `sandbox_unavailable` when there
is no sandbox to write into and `put_failed` when the bytes did not land.
declarations.name: put_file

parameters.documentation: The file to copy in; pass its handle object.
parameters.label: content

parameters.documentation: Where to write it inside the sandbox.
parameters.label: path

declarations.checkedType: agent(content_type?: string, path: string) -> file with session | throw[get_failed | sandbox_unavailable] | io
declarations.documentation:
Tool: take a file out of the Python sandbox — the only way anything the code produced (a chart, a CSV, a
report) leaves it. Give the @path@ the code wrote to, and @content_type@ the MIME type to record on the
result (e.g. "image/png", "text/csv") so whatever receives the file can display it; the sandbox
filesystem knows nothing about types, so leaving it out leaves the file untyped. Comes back as the `file`
itself, a handle to pass straight on to any tool that takes a file; it throws `sandbox_unavailable` when
there is no sandbox to read from and `get_failed` when nothing came out — read the message and try the
path the code actually wrote.
declarations.name: get_file

parameters.documentation: The path inside the sandbox to read.
